opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a tendency, especially in our community, to look at a benchmark result and treat it as if the economic or societal consequences follow almost automatically. The model can do the task in a realistic setting, so surely it's about to transform that sector. But there are a lot of steps between "capable in principle" and "actually changing how the world works."

One piece is reliability. Doing a task well 80 or 90 percent of the time in an evaluation is very different from doing it well enough that an organization will hand over responsibility for it. In many real settings, the cost of the failures dominates. If a system occasionally makes confident, strange errors, someone has to check its work, and once you account for that oversight the productivity gain can shrink a lot.

Then there's integration. Real tasks are embedded in workflows, legacy software, organizational processes, legal liability, and tacit knowledge that isn't written down anywhere. A lot of what a human employee does is context-gathering: knowing who to ask, what the unstated expectations are, what happened last quarter. Benchmarks usually hand the model a nicely packaged problem, and the world rarely does that.

There are institutional and social frictions too. Regulation, professional licensing, procurement cycles, union agreements, and simple trust all slow things down. Historically, general-purpose technologies like electricity or computing took decades to show up in productivity statistics, because firms had to reorganize themselves around the technology, not just bolt it on.

And there are complementary inputs. Impact often depends on things the AI doesn't control: physical infrastructure, data access, capital, people who know how to deploy it well.

None of that means the gap is permanent or that it will always be large. Some of these frictions can collapse quickly, especially if AI systems themselves get good at the integration work, or if competitive pressure forces fast adoption. That's part of why I think it's important to study the gap explicitly rather than assume it away in either direction. If you ignore it, you overestimate how fast things will move. If you treat it as fixed, you can be badly surprised when it closes.

r001.rationale: The response says failure costs and human oversight can shrink productivity gains, but does not clearly state that the cost of employing AI can make the task uneconomical in practice.

r002.rationale: The response identifies integration with workflows, legacy software, and organizational processes as factors between task capability and real-world impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Allan Dafoe: Yeah, so I think this is one of the most underappreciated points when people look at evaluations and benchmarks. We've gotten quite good at building evals where a model does something that looks like a real task — it writes a function, it drafts a legal memo, it answers a question a professional would answer. And the model passes. And then people say, well, that profession is about to be automated. And I think that inference skips over a lot.

The first thing is that a task in an eval is isolated and well-specified. Someone has already done the work of deciding what the problem is, gathering the relevant inputs, and defining what success looks like. In the real world, a huge fraction of the value of a skilled person is in that framing step — knowing which problem actually matters, knowing what context is relevant, noticing that the question as posed is slightly wrong. Evals mostly hand that to the model for free.

The second thing is that real-world impact is almost never a single task. It's a long chain of tasks embedded in an organization, with handoffs, feedback, trust relationships, accountability. If a model does ninety-five percent of the steps well but you can't rely on it for the other five, you may still need a human in the loop, and then the economic structure of the job doesn't change nearly as much as the benchmark suggests. Reliability matters a lot more than peak capability for actual deployment.

And then there's the whole set of frictions that have nothing to do with capability at all. Institutions have to decide to adopt the technology. There are liability questions, regulatory questions, questions of who gets blamed when something goes wrong. Workflows have to be redesigned. Complementary infrastructure has to be built. If you look historically at electricity or computers, there's this well-known lag of decades between the technology clearly working and productivity statistics actually moving. I don't think AI will take that long, but I don't think the lag is zero either.

So when I see a model do a realistic task, my reaction is: that's real information about capability, and it's an important leading indicator. But the mapping from "can do this in a controlled setting" to "is reshaping the world" runs through all these layers of integration, reliability, trust, and institutional change. And I think a lot of the forecasting disagreement in this field comes down to people having very different implicit models of how thick those layers are.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability, human oversight, and how job economics may change, but it does not explain that the cost of employing AI can make feasible performance uneconomical.

r002.rationale: It explains that adoption, workflow redesign, infrastructure, and institutional integration affect whether capability translates into real-world impact.

astra-6.text:
Well, performing a task is only one part of producing an outcome. You can show that an AI does something impressive in a fairly realistic setting, but there can still be a lot of work involved in making that capability useful in the world. Someone has to identify where to use it, integrate it into a workflow, check its outputs, and take responsibility when it makes mistakes.

And reliability matters enormously. A system that succeeds most of the time might be impressive as a demonstration, but if failures are difficult to detect or very costly, you may not be able to delegate much to it. You still need a human supervising it, and that can substantially reduce the benefit.

So I’d distinguish evidence that a model has a capability from evidence that we can deploy that capability at scale and achieve some consequential result. The first is relevant to the second, but there are complementary technologies, organizational changes, and institutional constraints in between. That gap can close quickly in some domains, but we shouldn’t assume that a realistic task demonstration means it has already closed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses integration work, oversight, and reliability, but does not say that the cost of employing AI can make feasible task performance uneconomical.

r002.rationale: It mentions integrating AI into a workflow and organizational or institutional constraints, but does not clearly identify compatibility with the existing ecosystem as a condition for real-world impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a lot of steps between demonstrating that an AI can do a task and that capability translating into impact. A realistic task can still be quite different from the situation you encounter in the world. The problem may be clearly specified, the relevant information may be supplied, and success may be relatively easy to assess. In practice, figuring out what to do, getting the information you need, and knowing whether you’ve succeeded can be a large part of the work.

Then there’s the question of integration. Can you make the system reliable enough that people will delegate to it? Does it fit into an organisation’s processes? Does someone have the incentive and authority to change those processes? A system might perform a particular task very well, but if that task isn’t the bottleneck, improving it may have relatively little effect on the overall outcome.

So I’d distinguish evidence of a capability from evidence that it can be deployed effectively, and then from evidence of substantial impact. The first can be very informative, but there’s quite a bit you need to understand before you can infer the third.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability, organizational processes, incentives, and bottlenecks, but does not say that the cost of employing AI can make feasible performance uneconomical.

r002.rationale: It says impact depends on whether the system fits into an organisation’s processes and whether those processes can change, identifying compatibility with the existing ecosystem as a condition.
